name: Carlos Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a big online home goods shop, answering calls and chats, mostly people asking where their order is. Sofas that didn't turn up, lamps that arrived broken, that sort of thing. The centre's above the shop's warehouse on the edge of town, so you can hear the forklifts all day. I like the people on my team and I like fixing a delivery for someone who's taken a day off work to wait. What wears me out is January, when they cut hours after Christmas.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do your hours change across the year?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In November and December I can do fifty hours a week with overtime, and then in January and February I'm down to thirty, sometimes twenty-five. I live with my older brother Luis in a rented house, and we split the bills, so a quiet month hurts. I use the AI summary tool now and then, when the order history is long, because it saves me reading twenty notes. I don't use it for everything, I want to see it work first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overblown, like most things online. At work I'd say the summary tool's handy, nothing more. I wouldn't post about it, I'm not really an online person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be stuck with the same problem, which is the hours. Every January the online shop cuts my hours after the Christmas rush, and no amount of AI hype changes that. I've got less than a month saved, and the bad months eat it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, and keep using the summary tool when it helps. I'd ask about a permanent full-time contract, because I'm still on a flexible one after four years. And I'd try to save from the Christmas overtime instead of spending it, so January doesn't bite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit flat. It's the same worry every winter, just without the AI on top. I'm used to it, but being used to it isn't the same as being fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What usually happens to the Christmas overtime money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What usually happens to the Christmas overtime money?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you pushed for the full-time contract before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It goes on Christmas, honestly, presents for my nieces and a trip to see my parents. Then the gas bill arrives. Luis says I should put half aside, and he's right, but I never quite manage it.

say: I'd say AI was **overblown**, like most things online.
At work I'd call the AI summary tool **handy**, nothing more.
think: His real problem is **January hours**, cut every year after Christmas.
He has **less than a month** saved, and the quiet months eat it.
do: Keep using the **summary tool** when order histories are long.
Ask for a **full-time contract** after four years flexible.
feel: **Uneasy** and flat, the same **winter worry** as always.
S0.quote: Every January the online shop cuts my hours after the Christmas rush, and no amount of AI hype changes that.
fieldNote: His pressure is **seasonal hours**, not AI.
He's on a **flexible contract** after four years and never pushed.
He spends overtime on **family** rather than saving it.

steps.text: Ask his manager for a permanent full-time contract
Put half the Christmas overtime pay into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's changing fast and people should get ready, not panic. At work I'd say learn the tools, because they're coming either way. With friends I'd be a bit quieter, because some of them work in the same place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's right in the firing line. Nine out of ten calls I take are people asking where their parcel is, and a computer already knows where their parcel is. They'd keep a few of us for the hard cases, and I'm average, so I'd say fifty-fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly, every day, to be one of the people who handles the hard cases. I'd look into a forklift licence, because the warehouse downstairs is always hiring and it's hands-on. I'd stop the takeaways and put a bit away every week, and I'd talk to Luis about whether we could manage if I lost hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd have something to do, which helps. It's like seeing a storm on the forecast: you can't stop it, you can bring the washing in. I'd still sleep worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the forklift licence, rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why the forklift licence, rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Luis say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can see the warehouse from my desk window, and they pay a bit more than me. It's a short course, a few days, and the shop sometimes pays for it. But the warehouse has robots on some lines already, so I'd want something beyond that too, maybe a lorry licence later.

say: I'd say people should **get ready**, not panic.
I'd tell colleagues to **learn the tools**, as they're coming anyway.
think: His order-tracking job on the phones is right **in the firing line**.
Being average, he puts his chances at **fifty-fifty**.
do: Use **AI tools** daily to qualify for hard cases.
Get a **forklift licence** for the warehouse downstairs.
feel: **Worried**, but steadier for having a plan.
Like bringing the washing in before a **storm**.
S1.quote: Nine out of ten calls I take are people asking where their parcel is, and a computer already knows where their parcel is.
fieldNote: He sees his **order-tracking** calls as the easiest work to automate.
His plan is a **forklift licence**, then maybe a lorry licence.
He hates the idea of **living off** his brother Luis.

steps.text: Use the AI order tools every shift to handle harder cases
Take the short forklift licence course for warehouse work
Stop takeaways and save a fixed amount each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to cope with, and the government needs to help people through it. At work I'd say get any hands-on skill you can, now. I'd probably start reading the news a lot more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job is gone in 2028 or before. Answering parcel questions is pure screen work, so I don't get the three years extra that hands-on jobs get. I'd have about eighteen months to get a lorry licence and save, while the work I do now disappears underneath me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, I'd book the forklift course and then a lorry licence, which takes a few months and costs money I'd have to borrow from Luis. Driving is hands-on, so it lasts till about 2031 on this card. I'd cut everything I could, and once the job goes I'd sign on for whatever support exists while I finish the licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but not frozen. I'd have a plan, it just wouldn't be a long one. Three years of driving and then what, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd borrow from Luis. How much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd borrow from Luis. How much?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after the three years of driving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lorry licence is a few thousand, which is more than I've ever had. Luis might have it, he's careful. I'd pay him back from the first wages, and I'd write it down so it doesn't sit between us.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government must help.
I'd tell colleagues to get **hands-on skills** now.
think: Screen work gives him **no extra three years**; the job goes by 2028.
Learning a **lorry licence** and saving must happen at once.
do: Book the **forklift course** and a lorry licence.
**Sign on** for support while finishing the licence.
S2.quote: I'd have about eighteen months to get a lorry licence and save, while the work I do now disappears underneath me.
fieldNote: He reads the **robot lag** correctly and aims for driving work.
He'd borrow from his brother Luis but **write it down**.
Beyond 2031 he has **no plan** at all.

steps.text: Book a forklift course, then a lorry licence
Borrow the licence fee from Luis and repay from first wages
Cut every non-essential bill straight away
Apply for job-loss support while finishing the licence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a sensible warning, and the shop should help people retrain. At work I'd be saying the same. I'd tell friends to save, which is funny coming from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years gives me a real shot. With five years I can get my lorry licence on weekends, keep the phone job going, and jump when the parcel calls dry up. Robots for driving come about 2034 here, so I'd have a few years behind the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd use the AI tools more at work and ask about the shop paying for a forklift course. In years two and three I'd do the lorry licence at weekends, paying monthly. I'd try to save from overtime properly this time, maybe a hundred a month in the busy season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can see the steps. It feels like a long walk rather than a cliff. I'd still have bad nights in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rather stay in customer service if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you rather stay in customer service if you could?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind about the lorry licence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, yes, I like people. But I'm not going to stay somewhere that's closing just because I like it. If a driving job means I talk to a few people a day, that'd be enough.

say: I'd call **five years** a sensible warning.
I'd say the online shop should help its agents with **retraining**.
think: Five years gives him a **real shot** at driving work.
Driving robots come around **2034**, leaving years behind the wheel.

S3.quote: With five years I can get my lorry licence on weekends, keep the phone job going, and jump when the parcel calls dry up.
fieldNote: He'd rather stay with **people**, but won't stay out of loyalty.
He'd check with his **cousin** before spending on the licence.
The **five-year** window turns panic into steps.

steps.text: Ask the shop to pay for a forklift course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, and there's no need to panic. At work I'd tell people to start thinking about it. With friends I'd probably not mention it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd lose this job at some point, but I'd have choices. Ten years is enough time to try two different jobs and pick the one I actually like, which I've never had the chance to do. I'd be thirty-seven when it arrives, and I'd want to be settled by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and use the AI tools when they make sense. I'd ask about moving into the warehouse or the delivery side within a couple of years, to try it out. And I'd start saving properly, even a little, because ten years of saving is real money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others. It's still there, but it's like knowing you'll need new tyres eventually. I'd worry more about January than about 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you try first?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move anywhere for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The delivery side, with the vans. I'd be out, I'd meet customers, I'd know the roads. If I hated it, I'd go back to the phones while they still exist.

say: I'd call **ten years** fair time, no need to panic.
I'd tell colleagues to **start thinking** about it.
think: He'd still **lose this job** at some point, but with real choices.
He'd want to be **settled** by thirty-seven.
do: Keep the job and use **AI tools** when sensible.
Try the **delivery side** within two years.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time to try two different jobs and pick the one I actually like, which I've never had the chance to do.
fieldNote: He has **never chosen** his work and sees ten years as a chance to.
**January hours** still worry him more than 2036.

steps.text: Keep the customer job and use AI tools where they help

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be learning to drive a lorry with no money while my job vanished. What would help is the cost of the licence covered for people who lose their jobs. And a clear picture of what jobs are left, so I'm not guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like to be on a flexible contract. I'm not scared of a machine knowing where a parcel is, I'm scared of a machine deciding I'm not needed to say it. That's the bit people don't think about.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of a machine knowing where a parcel is, I'm scared of a machine deciding I'm not needed to say it.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old** agent answering delivery queries for an online home goods shop.
He shares a rented house with his brother Luis and has **less than a month** saved.
He uses AI **now and then** and waits to see tools proven first.
His plan across scenarios is **hands-on driving**: forklift, then a lorry licence.
He moves from **anxious** to alarmed, easing back as warning time grows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, retraining with no money as his job vanishes.
whatWouldHelp: Help paying for a **lorry licence** after job loss.
A clear picture of **which jobs remain**.
